keywords: can I have a campfire in Yosemite

faq.q: Are campfires banned in Yosemite right now?
faq.a: Yosemite implemented Stage 1 fire restrictions at 12:01 a.m. on Friday, August 7, 2026, banning wood and charcoal fires, including twig stoves, parkwide below 8,000 feet. The restrictions remain in effect until further notice.

faq.q: What is the elevation line for Yosemite's fire restrictions?
faq.a: 8,000 feet in 2026. Below that elevation, wood and charcoal fires are banned outside a few exemptions. The line is set by the park's fire managers based on that year's conditions and has sat lower, closer to 6,000 feet, in some past seasons.

faq.q: Can I use a camp stove during Yosemite's fire restrictions?
faq.a: Yes. Portable stoves burning pressurized gas, liquid fuel, or propane are permitted, as are alcohol stoves, including small tablet or cube stoves. The restrictions ban wood and charcoal fires, not stoves.

faq.q: Can I have a campfire in a Yosemite campground during fire restrictions?
faq.a: Designated frontcountry campgrounds and picnic areas below 8,000 feet are exempt from the wood and charcoal ban, so an established fire ring at a campground like Upper Pines or Wawona can still hold a fire. In El Portal and Foresta, only charcoal fires are allowed, not wood.

faq.q: Is smoking banned in Yosemite during fire restrictions?
faq.a: Below 8,000 feet, smoking is prohibited except inside an enclosed vehicle, inside a campground or picnic area where fires are still permitted, or in a posted designated smoking area.

faq.q: Can I have a campfire while backpacking in Yosemite right now?
faq.a: Only in an existing fire ring between 8,000 and 9,600 feet. Above 9,600 feet, campfires are prohibited year-round because wood is scarce at that elevation. Most trailheads out of Tuolumne Meadows, Glacier Point Road, and the Valley rim start below 8,000 feet, so a stove is the reliable option for at least the first stretch of most routes.

faq.q: When do Yosemite's fire restrictions usually end?
faq.a: When temperatures drop and real rain falls, not on a fixed date. Yosemite has historically had close to a 90 percent chance of a season-ending precipitation event, two or more inches of rain, by October 31. Restrictions were lifted in September 2022 and in late October 2021 after rain, snow, and cooler temperatures reduced the fire danger.

keywords: how many days do you need in Yosemite

faq.q: Is three days enough for Yosemite?
faq.a: Yes, and it is the shortest visit that is. Three days covers Yosemite Valley, the Glacier Point rim, and the Tioga Road high country, one per day, without hurry. When a seasonal road is closed, that day's slot goes to Wawona and the Mariposa Grove or to Hetch Hetchy.

faq.q: How many days is ideal for a Yosemite trip?
faq.a: Four or five. Four adds Hetch Hetchy or one serious hike to the three-day core; five adds an unscheduled day, which sounds like padding and is usually the best day of the trip.

faq.q: Can you do Glacier Point and Tioga Road on the same day?
faq.a: You can drive it, but you should not: they point in opposite directions from the Valley and each is two to four hours of driving round trip. Combining them turns both into windshield scenery. One park per day.

faq.q: What order should the days go in?
faq.a: Valley first, the Glacier Point rim second, the Tioga high country third, then the far corner or the big hike. The Valley teaches you the park, the rim reuses that knowledge from above, and the high country needs the earliest start and the most settled weather.

faq.q: Does a multi-day Yosemite itinerary work in winter?
faq.a: A compressed version does: the Valley under snow, Badger Pass and the snowshoe rim at Dewey Point, then the Mariposa Grove on foot or Hetch Hetchy, which sits below four thousand feet and is often snow-free. Tioga Road and Glacier Point Road are closed in winter, typically November into May.

faq.q: Do I need a reservation to enter Yosemite in 2026?
faq.a: No. There is no day-use or peak-hours reservation in 2026. You need the $35 seven-day vehicle pass, and international visitors age 16 and up pay a $100 per-person surcharge in effect since January 1, 2026.

faq.q: Should I plan Half Dome into a three-to-five-day trip?
faq.a: Only as an upgrade, never as the spine. Permits are a lottery, preseason in March or daily two days ahead, so build day four to be good without the summit and let a winning application improve it.

keywords: Yosemite in winter what to do

faq.q: Can you hike in Yosemite in winter?
faq.a: Yes. The Valley floor trails stay open all season, Columbia Rock is a real 1,000-foot climb that melts out between storms, the Vernal Fall footbridge stays reachable by its winter route, and Hetch Hetchy and Wawona hike nearly all winter at their lower elevations.

faq.q: Is the Mist Trail open in winter?
faq.a: The granite stair beside Vernal Fall closes in winter, along with the John Muir Trail between Clark Point and the top of Nevada Fall, because of falling ice. The winter route runs to the Vernal Fall footbridge and, conditions allowing, to the top of Vernal via Clark Point. Nevada Fall has no winter walking route.

faq.q: Is the Four Mile Trail open in winter?
faq.a: No. It closes with the first lasting snow, typically into May, occasionally reopening its lowest miles to a gate below Union Point in lean spells.

faq.q: Do you need snowshoes to hike Yosemite in winter?
faq.a: Not on the Valley floor, at Hetch Hetchy, or in Wawona: boots with traction cleats for ice are the right tool there. Snowshoes earn their weight above the rim out of Badger Pass, and in the Mariposa Grove after fresh snow.

faq.q: What is the best winter hike in Yosemite?
faq.a: For effort against reward, Columbia Rock: about two miles round trip and 1,000 feet up the sunny south-facing wall. For solitude, the Wapama Falls trail at Hetch Hetchy, about five miles round trip. For the sight nobody expects, the two-mile walk up the closed road to the snowbound sequoias of the Mariposa Grove.

faq.q: Is Hetch Hetchy open for hiking in winter?
faq.a: Usually. It sits below four thousand feet and is the corner of the park most likely to be snow-free all winter. The access road runs on posted gate hours, roughly sunrise to sunset, and snow can close it for days after a storm, so check conditions before the drive.

keywords: camping in Yosemite for the first time

faq.q: What is a Yosemite campground actually like for a first-timer?
faq.a: Dense and social, not solitary. The three Yosemite Valley campgrounds hold roughly 380 sites between them, and Upper Pines alone holds well over half of those. You will see and hear your neighbors. The reason to camp anyway is the hours: you are inside the park for the ninety minutes after the day visitors leave and the ninety before they come back, which is when the Valley is worth being in.

faq.q: What is in a Yosemite campsite?
faq.a: A numbered dirt or gravel pad, a picnic table, a steel fire ring with a grate, and a metal food locker. That is the whole inventory. There are no hookups of any kind, no electricity, and no water at the site, and no Yosemite campground has showers. The nearest public showers are at Curry Village for about five dollars, with a long peak-season line.

faq.q: What has to go in the bear box at a Yosemite campsite?
faq.a: Anything with a smell, not just food. Food, drinks, the cooler itself even when empty, toothpaste, sunscreen, lip balm, bug spray, soap, dish rags, and trash. Nothing scented stays in the car overnight. The usual failure is not ignorance but the latch: a closed unlatched box is an open box to a bear. Improper storage carries fines reaching five thousand dollars.

faq.q: How cold does it get camping in Yosemite in summer?
faq.a: It depends entirely on which part of the park. Yosemite Valley sits at about 4,000 feet and is mild on a July night. Tuolumne Meadows sits at about 8,600 feet and can drop into the high thirties on the same date. Look up your specific campground's elevation rather than the park's, and treat a published forecast low as optimistic, since cold air pools in low ground overnight.

faq.q: What are the quiet hours and generator hours in Yosemite campgrounds?
faq.a: Quiet hours run from 10 PM to 6 AM. Generators are permitted only from 7 to 9 in the morning, noon to 2, and 5 to 7 in the evening. Check-in and check-out are both around noon, which means your site may still be occupied if you arrive at eleven. In the summer months, wood fires in Yosemite Valley are restricted to evening hours for air quality.

faq.q: Do I still pay the park entrance fee if I have a camping reservation?
faq.a: Yes. A campground reservation is not park entry. The entrance fee is $35 per vehicle, good for seven days, and the entrance stations are cashless. Budget for it separately.

faq.q: Does a Yosemite wilderness permit mean my route is passable?
faq.a: No. The permit reserves a trailhead and a start date, not a campsite and not a condition report. It does not certify that a pass is clear of snow, that a bridge is standing, or that a ford is safe. The park meters the first day and leaves the rest to your own judgment, which makes conditions research your job rather than the agency's.

faq.q: When does the snow melt out of the Yosemite high country?
faq.a: Later than the road opening suggests. Tioga Road tops out at 9,945 feet and gets plowed; the passes on your route do not. In a normal year, a route that holds you above about 9,500 feet is a gamble in June and stops being one in early July. Aspect matters as much as elevation: two slopes at the same altitude can be bare granite and rotten snow depending on which way they face.

faq.q: When are creek crossings dangerous in Yosemite?
faq.a: Peak runoff generally runs from late May into June, shifting earlier in a low-snow year and later in a big one. It also moves through the day: snowmelt creeks run lowest in the early morning, before the sun has worked on the snowfields upstream, and highest in the late afternoon and evening. A crossing you would refuse at four in the afternoon is often unremarkable at seven the next morning.

faq.q: When is mosquito season in the Yosemite high country?
faq.a: Mosquitoes emerge from snowmelt water roughly a couple of weeks after a given elevation band melts out, so the peak is a wave that climbs the mountain rather than a date. Broadly the worst of it runs from about mid-June into early July across the elevations you can drive to, eases through late July, and is largely finished by September. In a low-snow year the whole sequence shifts earlier.

faq.q: Is a bear canister required for backpacking in Yosemite?
faq.a: Yes, parkwide for any overnight wilderness stay. Hanging food is not an accepted alternative here. Yosemite also maintains its own approved-container list that is narrower than the certifications other agencies accept, and soft-sided bag-style containers of the Ursack type are not on it. Confirm your specific model against the park's current list, or rent a canister from a wilderness center for a few dollars a week plus a refundable deposit.

faq.q: What are good first backpacking trips in Yosemite?
faq.a: Cathedral Lakes from Tuolumne Meadows, roughly four and a half miles in and nine or so round trip, with a thousand to 1,400 feet of cumulative gain. Sunrise Lakes from Tenaya Lake, about seven and a half miles round trip with roughly 1,400 feet. Glen Aulin, about eleven miles round trip but only around 800 feet of elevation change. And Little Yosemite Valley from Happy Isles, under ten miles round trip with about 2,000 feet of gain.

keywords: Yosemite day trip from San Francisco
Yosemite day trip from Bay Area
San Francisco to Yosemite drive time
is Yosemite worth a day trip
Yosemite day trip without a car

faq.q: How long does it really take to drive from San Francisco to Yosemite Valley?
faq.a: Four to five hours each way is the honest planning figure from San Francisco, Oakland, or San Jose. Routing apps quote something in the region of three and a half hours, which assumes an empty I-580, no stops, no entrance line, and no slowing for the curves on the New Priest Grade. Call it nine hours of driving for the round trip and you will not be disappointed.

faq.q: Is Yosemite worth a day trip from the Bay Area?
faq.a: It works under narrow conditions. Around the summer solstice the Valley gets close to fifteen hours of daylight, so a five in the morning departure buys seven or eight hours in the park across a seventeen-hour day. Around the winter solstice the same trip buys about five hours, half of them in flat light, with the last stretch of the drive home in the dark. Midweek is the difference between the trip working and not working.

faq.q: Do I need a reservation to enter Yosemite in 2026?
faq.a: No. The day-use reservation systems that ran from 2020 through 2025 are gone and you simply drive up. What that changed is where the queue forms rather than whether it exists: on peak summer weekends entrance lines run an hour or more from mid-morning, and the Valley day-use lots have been reported full between seven and eight in the morning on the busiest days.

faq.q: What can you actually do in Yosemite in one day?
faq.a: One part of the park, not the park. A workable Valley day is Tunnel View on the way in, then parking once and using the free shuttle for Lower Yosemite Fall, the Cook's Meadow Loop, Bridalveil Fall, a packed lunch, and El Capitan Meadow with binoculars. Adding Glacier Point costs two hours of driving and Mariposa Grove costs three or more, so each is the whole day rather than an addition.

faq.q: Can you get to Yosemite from the Bay Area without a car?
faq.a: Yes. Amtrak's San Joaquins run to Merced, with a bus connection from San Francisco to Emeryville and a BART interchange at Richmond, and YARTS buses run from the Merced station up Highway 140 into Yosemite Valley year-round, timed to the trains and bookable as a single ticket. You skip the entrance line and the parking problem, but combined transit runs roughly four to four and a half hours each way and the schedule decides when you leave.

faq.q: What does a Yosemite day trip cost from the Bay Area?
faq.a: A round trip from San Francisco is close to four hundred miles, so fuel runs somewhere in the region of seventy to a hundred dollars depending on the vehicle, plus the $35 per-vehicle entrance fee. The fee is the buried point: it covers seven days, so a day-tripper pays the full $35 for one day while an overnight visitor pays the same $35 for two or three.

keywords: is it safe to swim in Yosemite

faq.q: Can you swim in the Merced River in Yosemite?
faq.a: Yes. Swimming is permitted in the Merced through Yosemite Valley, but there are no lifeguards anywhere on the river, there is no designated swimming area, and the Park Service asks visitors to enter and leave the water only at sandy beaches. Swimming is prohibited outright in a specific list of other places, including Emerald Pool and the Silver Apron above Vernal Fall.

faq.q: When is it safe to swim in the Merced River?
faq.a: Not during the spring melt. Through the runoff the current is stronger than it looks and the water is cold enough to disable a strong adult in under a minute. As a rough shape of the year the swimming season runs from about mid-July into September, and in June the answer is almost always not yet, but the changeover moves several weeks in either direction with the snowpack. In a heavy year the river can still be running spring volumes well into July, so check the flow on the day rather than trusting a date.

faq.q: Where are the best swimming spots on the Merced in Yosemite Valley?
faq.a: Sentinel Beach is the default: a sandy bank on the south side with a picnic area attached, calm by late summer, and the one to take small children to. Cathedral Beach downstream is wider and deeper with El Capitan upstream in the view, better for adults who want to actually swim. Devil's Elbow on Northside Drive comes good once the river drops, and the Swinging Bridge shallows are the best wading water in the Valley for toddlers. Wawona on the South Fork has the warmest swimming in the park; Tenaya Lake on Tioga Road has the coldest.

faq.q: Where is swimming prohibited in Yosemite?
faq.a: Emerald Pool and the Silver Apron above Vernal Fall, Hetch Hetchy Reservoir and the first mile up its tributaries, the Dana Fork of the Tuolumne River, Lake Eleanor where posted, and the Wawona domestic water intake and the hundred yards above it. These are rules rather than advice. Beyond the posted list, never swim above any waterfall at any flow: the current accelerates toward the lip in ways you cannot feel and the granite under it is polished.

faq.q: Why is cold water dangerous even for strong swimmers?
faq.a: Because the dangerous part happens in the first minute, not the first hour. Going into cold water triggers an involuntary gasp followed by breathing you cannot control, and if your head is under at that moment you inhale water. Over the following minutes your hands and forearms stop doing what you ask of them, well before you feel dangerously cold. People do not drown in snowmelt because they are bad swimmers; they drown because the ability to swim is temporarily taken away from them. Get in gradually rather than jumping, and never enter cold water alone.

faq.q: Do you need a life jacket to raft the Merced River in Yosemite?
faq.a: Children aged thirteen and under must wear one on the water at all times. Everyone must wear one when the Pohono Bridge gauge reads above four feet at eight in the morning. Boating is also restricted above Little Yosemite Valley and below El Capitan Bridge. That four-foot threshold is worth knowing even if you are only swimming: if the river is high enough that the Park Service has made flotation compulsory for rafters, it is not a swimming day.

faq.q: How long does it take to drive from Yosemite Valley to Tuolumne Meadows?
faq.a: Roughly 55 to 60 miles on Tioga Road, which is about an hour and a half each way in no traffic and closer to two hours in July. That is three to four hours of driving bracketing your day, and it is the number that quietly ruins Tuolumne itineraries. Leave the Valley early rather than mid-morning.

faq.q: Is there gas at Tuolumne Meadows?
faq.a: No. The old station has been out of operation for years and travel sites still list it. Inside the park on the west side, Crane Flat is the only fuel and is pay-at-pump around the clock. On the east side your next fuel is Lee Vining, about forty-five minutes past the meadows. Fill up at Crane Flat on the way in whether or not you think you need to.

faq.q: What can you do at Tuolumne Meadows if you are not a hiker?
faq.a: A great deal, because at 8,600 feet you are already standing in the view. The Olmsted Point nature trail is half a mile round trip with a hundred feet of climb. Pothole Dome is a mile round trip and buys the entire sweep of the meadows for ten minutes of easy climbing on glacier-polished granite. Soda Springs and Parsons Memorial Lodge is a mile and a half, flat, on an old road. The Tenaya Lake loop is two and a half miles and level, with a real sand beach at the east end.

faq.q: How high is Tuolumne Meadows and will the altitude affect you?
faq.a: Tuolumne Meadows sits at about 8,600 feet, more than 4,500 feet above the Yosemite Valley floor, and Tioga Pass is 9,945 feet. Altitude usually shows up not as dramatic mountain sickness but as an afternoon headache, a shorter temper, and a walk that felt much harder than a mile should. Drink more water than you want to, eat more than you planned, go slower on the first walk of the day, and if a headache will not shift, drive back down.

faq.q: When is Tioga Road open?
faq.a: Tioga Road opened on May 15 in 2026, unusually early. In a typical year it opens in late May or early June and closes with the first serious snow in late October or November. The date moves with the snowpack every year, so check current conditions rather than planning around an average.

faq.q: Are afternoon thunderstorms a problem in the Yosemite high country?
faq.a: In July and August the high country builds thunderstorms out of a clear morning with startling speed: clear at dawn, cumulus stacking by late morning, lightning possible from early afternoon. Plan the day around it by doing the exposed thing first. Domes, summits and open granite in the morning; meadow, forest, lakeshore and lunch in the afternoon. Carry a rain shell even when the morning makes it look ridiculous.

faq.q: Can you drive to the Mariposa Grove?
faq.a: Not in season, and not since 2018. Private vehicles park at the Mariposa Grove Welcome Plaza just inside the South Entrance, and a free shuttle covers the two miles up Mariposa Grove Road to the Arrival Area. The road beyond the plaza is closed to private cars while the shuttle is running. The one exception is a vehicle displaying a disability placard, which may drive the road.

faq.q: How does the Mariposa Grove shuttle work?
faq.a: It is free, there is no ticket, and individual riders need no reservation. Buses run roughly every fifteen minutes between the Welcome Plaza and the Arrival Area, take about ten minutes, and are wheelchair accessible with lifts and tie-downs. The Park Service does not publish hard season dates, saying only that it begins no earlier than April 15 and ends on or before November 30. Check the posted hours at the plaza, and note the last downhill departure before you walk away from the stop.

faq.q: Where do you park for the Mariposa Grove?
faq.a: At the Mariposa Grove Welcome Plaza, which is the first right at the roundabout just inside the South Entrance on Highway 41, less than a quarter mile in. It holds a few hundred vehicles and fills on busy days. There are restrooms and a Yosemite Conservancy bookstore there, and no food service anywhere in the grove.

faq.q: Are dogs allowed in the Mariposa Grove?
faq.a: No. Dogs are not allowed on any trail in the Mariposa Grove, including the paved ones, and are not allowed on the shuttle. This is an explicit exception to Yosemite's general policy of permitting leashed dogs on paved trails, and it catches people out because the Tuolumne Grove on Highway 120 does permit them on its paved section. Leashed dogs are fine in the parking lot, which in practice means one adult stays with the car.

faq.q: How long do you need at the Mariposa Grove?
faq.a: Two hours is an absolute floor, and that only buys the shuttle both ways and the Big Trees Loop, which is three tenths of a mile, paved and wheelchair accessible. Half a day is right for the Grizzly Giant Loop, about two miles, with time to stand around. A full day is the upper grove. Add about an hour and a quarter each way if you are driving from Yosemite Valley.

faq.q: Can you visit the Mariposa Grove in winter?
faq.a: Yes, on foot. Mariposa Grove Road closes to vehicles at the end of November and reopens when the snow allows, which has meant anywhere from early April onward in recent years. The grove itself does not close: the road and trails stay open to foot travel, and walking, snowshoeing or skiing the two miles up from the South Entrance is one of the quietest good days available in Yosemite in February. Note that this is not a designated snow-play area; the park's sledding hill is at Crane Flat.

faq.q: Where do you park in Yosemite Valley?
faq.a: Yosemite Valley has three day-use parking areas: Yosemite Village, Yosemite Falls on Northside Drive by Yosemite Valley Lodge, and Curry Village in the east Valley. The Park Service's own advice is to park at one of the three and then see the Valley by free shuttle, bike path, and trail. If you have no particular plan, aim at Yosemite Village, because it is the hub the shuttle radiates from.

faq.q: What time does parking fill up in Yosemite Valley?
faq.a: The Park Service does not name an hour, only that during the busy summer season, especially on weekends, parking fills early. It names a window instead: most vehicle congestion happens between 10 a.m. and 6 p.m., with an official recommendation to be inside the park before 9 a.m. or to arrive after 5 p.m. Treat that as the outer bound. On a busy day the lots fill before the congestion window opens, so be through the gate by 8 a.m., and before 7 on a summer weekend. On a July or August Saturday the Valley lots are effectively gone by mid-morning; on a Tuesday in October you can often park at noon.

faq.q: What do you do if Yosemite Valley parking is full?
faq.a: Stop circling and take the next legal space you see, even in the wrong lot, because a shuttle ride costs less time than another lap. If everything is full, leave and come back at five, when the day-trippers are going home. Or go somewhere that is not the Valley: promoting recreation outside Yosemite Valley is now part of the park's own congestion strategy.

faq.q: Is there parking at the Mist Trail trailhead?
faq.a: No. Happy Isles, where the Mist Trail begins, is a shuttle stop rather than a parking area, and Mirror Lake is the same. Most of the Valley's famous trailheads have no lot at all. Park in one of the three day-use lots and ride to the trailhead.

faq.q: Do you need a reservation to drive into Yosemite in 2026?
faq.a: No. There is no day-use or peak-hours vehicle reservation for 2026, including the February weekends for Horsetail Fall, which carried one for four straight years before this season. The park replaced it with operational measures: real-time traffic monitoring, active parking management in the Valley, more staff at key intersections at peak periods, road-condition alerts, and a push toward weekday visits and toward areas outside Yosemite Valley.

faq.q: Can you park an RV in Yosemite Valley?
faq.a: Vehicles over 45 feet are not permitted on the roads into Yosemite Valley at all. Highway 140 through the Merced canyon is the forgiving approach, with no tunnels and roughly 60 feet of combined length allowed; the tunnels on Highways 41 and 120 drop to about 10 feet 2 inches of clearance at the curb. In the Valley, Curry Village has RV parking near its eastbound shuttle stop, but the better answer is to leave the rig at the campground and take the shuttle.

faq.q: Is the Yosemite Valley shuttle free?
faq.a: Yes. There is no ticket, pass, or reservation. You stand at a marked stop, board, and get off wherever you like. It runs daily from 7 a.m. to 10 p.m.

faq.q: How often does the Yosemite Valley shuttle run?
faq.a: There are two routes, both starting from Yosemite Village. The Valleywide Shuttle covers roughly nineteen stops across the whole Valley and comes about every 22 to 32 minutes. The East Valley Shuttle is a shorter loop serving Yosemite Village, Curry Village, the Pines campgrounds, and the east-Valley trailheads, and comes about every 18 to 22 minutes.

faq.q: Does the YARTS fare include the Yosemite entrance fee?
faq.a: The two official sources currently disagree. Park Service pages say riders arriving by YARTS do not pay the entrance fee, while the YARTS fares page says applicable Yosemite entrance and non-resident fees are not included and remain each passenger's responsibility. Budget as though you will pay it, and treat being waved through as a bonus. If you hold an America the Beautiful pass the question is moot.

faq.q: How do you get to Yosemite without a car?
faq.a: YARTS runs year-round on Highway 140 from the Amtrak station in Merced, through Mariposa, Midpines, and El Portal, about two and a half hours to Yosemite Valley. Seasonal routes run from Fresno on Highway 41, Sonora on Highway 120, and Mammoth Lakes and Lee Vining over Tioga Pass. All of them set down in the Valley on the free shuttle line.

faq.q: Do you have to take the shuttle to Mariposa Grove?
faq.a: In season, effectively yes. When the free grove shuttle is running, the road above the Welcome Plaza is closed to private cars, so you park at the plaza and ride about two miles up, with buses roughly every fifteen minutes. A vehicle displaying a disability placard may drive the grove road instead.

faq.q: Is taking the bus cheaper than driving to Yosemite?
faq.a: For one or two people on a Valley-focused trip, yes: a Merced round trip runs in the mid-forties for an adult at current summer rates, against fuel, the entrance fee, and the parking problem. For a family of four it usually is not, because four per-person fares cost several times a single vehicle entrance fee. Driving also wins for dawn starts and for trips spread across Glacier Point, Tuolumne, and Hetch Hetchy.

keywords: do you need a permit to hike in Yosemite

faq.q: Can you get a Yosemite wilderness permit the same day?
faq.a: Not online. Forty percent of each trailhead's daily quota is released on Recreation.gov at 7 a.m. Pacific seven days before the entry date, and the park's published reservation window stops taking online bookings a few days out, three by its own reckoning, so there is no booking tonight for a walk that starts tomorrow. Past that cutoff, unclaimed quota can be issued in person at a wilderness center on the start date, but the Park Service's own warning is that few, if any, unused permits will be available. Ask the desk what exists rather than naming the trailhead you wanted.

faq.q: Do you need a permit to day hike in Yosemite?
faq.a: No, with one exception. Every trail in the park is open without a permit today, including the Mist Trail, Yosemite Falls, the Four Mile, Cathedral Lakes, and Clouds Rest. The exception is Half Dome whenever the cables are up.

faq.q: Can you hike Half Dome without a permit?
faq.a: No. Permits are required every day the cables are up, rangers check them at a checkpoint below the subdome, and hiking past it without one is a citation. You can hike to the base of the subdome without a permit, and the view from there is worth the walk.

faq.q: How does the Half Dome daily lottery work?

faq.q: What animals can you see in Yosemite?

faq.q: When is the best time to see wildlife in Yosemite?

faq.q: Are there grizzly bears in Yosemite?
faq.a: No. Every bear in Yosemite is a black bear, whatever its color, and most are brown, cinnamon, or blond. There has not been a grizzly in California for a century; the animal survives only on the state flag. The park's black bear population is estimated at 300 to 500.

faq.q: How far away do you have to stay from wildlife in Yosemite?
faq.a: At least 50 yards from bears and at least 25 yards from all other wildlife, including deer. If an animal changes its behavior because of you, you are too close regardless of distance. Feeding any wild animal is illegal, and food-storage violations carry fines up to $5,000.

faq.q: What is the most dangerous animal in Yosemite?
faq.a: By injury count, the mule deer. Deer injure more visitors in Yosemite than bears do, mostly because people approach them for photographs. They are wild 150-pound animals with antlers and hooves; photograph them from the trail at 25 yards or more.

faq.q: Where can you see a great gray owl in Yosemite?
faq.a: Yosemite holds the southernmost breeding population of the great gray owl, which hunts the edges of mid-elevation meadows such as those near Crane Flat and Glacier Point Road at dawn and dusk. If you find one, keep your distance and never play recorded calls: playback harasses a state-endangered bird and is prohibited.

faq.q: When does showy milkweed bloom in Yosemite Valley?
faq.a: Roughly late June through July on the Valley floor, with mid-July near the peak. By August the flowers give way to warty seed pods that split open to release seeds carried on silky white floss. Showy milkweed favors open, sunny ground: it grows out through the Valley's big meadows, Cook's Meadow among the best, as well as along roadside verges and old pullouts.

faq.q: How do you identify showy milkweed?
faq.a: Look for a stout, waist-high perennial two to five feet tall with a fuzzy stem, broad opposite leaves that feel felted underneath, and rounded umbels of dusty pink to rose star-shaped flowers. Break a leaf or stem and it bleeds thick white latex. Each flower has five backward-curved petals below a crown of five pointed hoods, each hood holding a small curved horn.

faq.q: How is milkweed pollinated?
faq.a: Milkweed does not shed loose pollen. Its pollen is packaged in tiny saddlebag-shaped sacs called pollinia, joined in pairs by a clip. When a visiting bee, wasp, or butterfly slips a leg into a groove between the flower's hoods, the clip catches it and the insect carries the pollinia to the next flower. The mechanism is precise but inefficient: a whole umbel of dozens of flowers often sets only one or two seed pods.

faq.q: Why is milkweed important for monarch butterflies?
faq.a: Monarchs are an obligate specialist on milkweed: females lay eggs only on milkweed and the caterpillars eat only its leaves, so without milkweed there are no monarchs. The caterpillars also store the plant's cardiac glycoside toxins in their bodies, which makes both the caterpillar and the adult butterfly poisonous to predators. The western monarch has declined steeply, and the loss of breeding milkweed across the West is a leading cause.

faq.q: Is milkweed poisonous, and can you touch it?
faq.a: Milkweed's white latex contains cardiac glycosides that are toxic if eaten and that deter most grazing animals. The sap is a mild skin and eye irritant, so if you handle a broken stem, keep it away from your face and wash your hands afterward. Do not eat any part of it.

faq.q: Can you pick or transplant milkweed in Yosemite?
faq.a: No. Collecting or digging up plants is prohibited in Yosemite National Park, and a picked milkweed is a monarch nursery removed from the landscape. If you want milkweed at home, buy nursery stock of a species native to your own area rather than taking it from the wild.

Famous trailheads disappear in minutes, but less famous ones often linger for days, and unclaimed quota exists most days if you are flexible about where you start.

faq.q: Can I climb Half Dome on a wilderness permit?
faq.a: If your route plausibly passes Half Dome, you can request Half Dome access as an add-on to a wilderness permit for $10 per person, subject to its own daily cap. For many hikers this beats the day-hiker lottery odds.

faq.q: Is a bear canister required in the Yosemite Wilderness?

faq.q: Which Yosemite trails are wheelchair accessible?

faq.q: Is the Yosemite Valley shuttle wheelchair accessible?
faq.a: Yes. The free Valley shuttle has ramps and securement points and runs a loop of about nineteen stops covering the lodges, campgrounds, trailheads, and visitor center, roughly 7 a.m. to 10 p.m.

faq.q: Can I drive to the Mariposa Grove with a disability placard?

faq.q: Does Yosemite have ASL interpreters?
faq.a: Yes. American Sign Language interpretation is available for ranger programs; in the off-season, request an interpreter at least two weeks ahead (yose_deaf_services@nps.gov, or 209-379-5250 by voice or text). A public videophone for Deaf visitors is in the lobby of Yosemite Valley Lodge, and the park's films run captioned.

faq.q: What is the Access Pass?
faq.a: A free lifetime pass for U.S. citizens and permanent residents with a permanent disability. It admits the pass holder and everyone in the vehicle to every national park and federal recreation site, discounts about half the cost of most federal campgrounds, and replaces the $35 gate fee. It is available at the entrance station with documentation.

faq.q: Are dogs allowed on trails in Yosemite?
faq.a: With two exceptions, no. Leashed dogs are allowed only on the Wawona Meadow Loop and on Old Big Oak Flat Road between Hodgdon Meadow and Hazel Green Creek. Every other trail, along with meadows, the wilderness, shuttle buses, beaches, lodging, and public buildings, is off limits.

faq.q: Where can I take my dog in Yosemite?
faq.a: On fully paved roads, sidewalks, and bike paths (unless posted otherwise), in developed areas, and in most drive-in campgrounds, always on a leash no longer than six feet. The paved Valley Loop bike paths are the best dog walking in the park.

faq.q: Which Yosemite campgrounds allow dogs?
faq.a: Most drive-in campgrounds allow pets. The exceptions are Camp 4, all walk-in sites, and all group sites. Pet food and bowls must be stored in the bear box, exactly like human food, and dogs must be attended and leashed at your site.

faq.q: Can I leave my dog in the car in Yosemite?
faq.a: Not in warm weather, which in a Valley parking lot means most daylight hours from May through September. Citations run up to $5,000. Kennels in the gateway towns of Oakhurst and Mariposa are the workable alternative; book ahead in peak season.

faq.q: Are service animals allowed on Yosemite trails?
faq.a: Yes. Service dogs as the ADA defines them, individually trained to perform tasks for a person with a disability, may accompany their handlers on trails, in lodging, and on shuttles. Emotional support animals are not service animals under the ADA and receive no exemption.

faq.q: Are Yosemite ranger programs free?
faq.a: Yes. Ranger walks, talks, and evening amphitheater programs, led by uniformed NPS staff and volunteers, are free. The Yosemite Conservancy's guided experiences and the concessioner's commercial tours are separate, paid offerings.

faq.q: How do I find the Yosemite ranger program schedule?

faq.q: How does the Yosemite Junior Ranger program work?

faq.q: Can adults do the Yosemite Junior Ranger program?

faq.q: Are there ranger programs in Yosemite in winter?

faq.q: How do I get a camping reservation in Yosemite?

There are no hookups anywhere in the park.

faq.q: How do I get a Yosemite campsite when everything is sold out?
faq.a: Play the cancellation game. Cancellations spike about 14 days out, three to five days out, and the day before arrival. Set up free alert tools like Campflare or Outdoorithm, or the faster paid Campnab ($10 to $30 per month), to watch recreation.gov, be flexible on dates, and check manually during those windows. If you can take any three nights in a two-week range, your odds improve dramatically.

faq.q: What are the food storage rules at Yosemite campgrounds?
faq.a: Every campsite has a metal bear box, and everything with a scent goes in it, 24 hours a day: food, coolers, cooking utensils, toothpaste, sunscreen, lip balm, even the trail mix in your glove compartment. Nothing scented stays in your car. Rangers enforce this with fines up to $5,000, and a food-conditioned bear is eventually euthanized, so careless storage can kill a bear.

faq.q: Are there showers at Yosemite campgrounds?
faq.a: No. None of the campgrounds have showers. The nearest are the pay showers at Curry Village, which charge $5, with long lines in peak season. Most campers rely on baby wipes.

faq.q: Which Yosemite campground is best?
faq.a: It depends on what you value. Crane Flat is the versatile pick, cooler and quieter than the Valley, about 45 minutes to the Valley floor and an hour to Tuolumne Meadows. For the classic Valley experience, book a riverside site in Upper Pines (Loops E and F) or North Pines (the 500 series). For solitude, primitive campgrounds like Tamarack Flat and Yosemite Creek trade amenities for privacy.

faq.q: When can you camp in the Yosemite high country?
faq.a: When the Tioga Road opens. Plowing starts around the middle of April and takes a month or two, which usually puts the opening in late May or early June, though a heavy winter can push it well past that. The road opening is not the campground opening: Tuolumne Meadows, White Wolf, Yosemite Creek, Tamarack Flat, and Porcupine Flat come online in the weeks that follow, once water and sanitation are running, so July is the honest planning assumption for most of them. Nights are cold: Tuolumne at 8,600 feet can drop into the 30s in July, so bring a sleeping bag rated to at least 20 degrees.

faq.q: How dangerous are Yosemite's black bears?
faq.a: Yosemite has recorded zero fatal bear attacks in its history, going back to 1890. Across North America, black bears kill fewer than one person per year. The Merced River, the granite, and driving tired on park roads are all more dangerous than the bears.

faq.q: What should I do if I see a bear in Yosemite?
faq.a: Stand up, face the bear, raise your arms to look larger, and yell aggressively until it leaves. Never run (black bears can hit 35 mph) and never climb a tree (they climb better than you). Then report the encounter to the park at 209-372-0322, even if nothing happened.

faq.q: What counts as food under Yosemite's storage rules?
faq.a: All food, all coolers (including empty ones), trash, toiletries, sunscreen, lip balm, insect repellent, deodorant, and medications. faq.q: Which Yosemite trails are most dangerous in the heat?

faq.q: How much water should I carry hiking Yosemite in summer?
faq.a: The NPS baseline is one quart per hour of hiking in the heat. A full day on an exposed trail in July means 4 to 6 liters per person. Pair it with electrolytes or salty snacks: drinking large amounts of plain water without replacing sodium can cause hyponatremia, which mimics heat exhaustion.

faq.q: When is it safe to swim in the Merced River in Yosemite?
faq.a: Roughly mid-July through mid-September, once snowmelt drops and the water warms. Do not swim in May or June, when the river is high, fast, and cold; most river fatalities in Yosemite happen during the high-water period. Never swim above a waterfall.

faq.q: Where can you swim in Yosemite?

faq.q: How do you stay safe from afternoon thunderstorms in Yosemite?
faq.a: Be off exposed ridges, peaks, and open granite by noon. Sierra afternoon thunderstorms build like clockwork in July and August, often producing lightning by 1 PM. If you hear thunder above treeline you are already in strike range: get below treeline, off water, and crouch low with your feet together. The monsoon pattern runs from mid-July through September.

faq.q: How much cooler is Tuolumne Meadows than Yosemite Valley?

faq.q: Do you need chains to drive to Yosemite in March?

faq.q: Are the waterfalls flowing in Yosemite in March?

Cold March mornings can also produce frazil ice, a slush of ice crystals that flows down Yosemite Creek below Lower Yosemite Fall before about 9 a.m.

faq.q: Can you see the firefall in March?

faq.q: How crowded is Yosemite in March?

faq.q: Where is the Cathedral Lakes trailhead?

faq.q: What is the best time to hike Cathedral Lakes?

faq.q: Is the Cathedral Lakes hike crowded?

faq.q: How do you get to the Cathedral Lakes trailhead?

faq.q: How crowded is Yosemite Valley on Memorial Day weekend?

faq.q: How hard is the Four Mile Trail and Panorama Trail loop?
faq.a: Strenuous. The full loop is about 13 miles and gains 3,200 feet, almost all of it in the first 4.6 miles up the Four Mile Trail. The Panorama Trail descent is more gradual. Fit hikers take 7-10 hours. It is manageable for experienced day hikers; it is not a casual walk.

faq.q: How do I set up the Four Mile / Panorama Trail loop?

faq.q: Is there parking at the Four Mile Trailhead?

faq.q: Can I take the Glacier Point bus to do this hike one-way?
faq.a: Yes. The Glacier Point bus tour runs daily in summer from Yosemite Valley, and it fills quickly, so book in advance. Ride up, hike the Panorama Trail down to the Valley, and take the free shuttle back to your car. This gives you a point-to-point mostly-downhill hike.

faq.q: What are the best hikes for kids in Yosemite?
faq.a: For young children: the Lower Yosemite Fall loop (1 mile, paved, nearly flat), the Valley bike path, and the Mirror Lake loop (5 miles, flat). Older kids can do the Vernal Fall footbridge (1.6 miles, moderate). Avoid the Mist Trail above the footbridge with children under 10 - the wet granite stairs are genuinely dangerous in spring and early summer.

faq.q: Does Yosemite offer a Junior Ranger program for kids?

faq.q: Can I take YARTS to Yosemite with kids?
faq.a: Yes, and with young children it is often easier than driving. YARTS runs from Merced (with an Amtrak connection), Mariposa, and in summer from the east side via Tioga Road. Kids 12 and under ride free on the Highway 140/Merced route. Inside the park, the free Valley Shuttle connects all major stops.

faq.q: What age is appropriate for Yosemite with kids?
faq.a: Any age with realistic expectations. Infants and toddlers do well in a carrier on short paved walks. Kids 4-7 can handle 2-3 miles on flat valley trails. By 8-10 most kids can manage the Mist Trail to Vernal Fall. Teenagers can handle summit hikes like Sentinel Dome and the full Mist Trail to Nevada Fall.

faq.q: Do I need reservations for Yosemite with kids in 2026?
faq.a: No day-use vehicle reservation is required in 2026. Summer campground reservations on Recreation.gov book out months in advance and are essential. In-park lodging fills 6-12 months ahead. YARTS does not require advance booking, though popular runs fill on peak weekends.

faq.q: What is the elevation of Tioga Pass?

faq.q: Do I need a reservation to enter Yosemite in 2026?

faq.q: How long does it take to drive Tioga Road?
faq.a: Tioga Road runs about 39 miles from Crane Flat to Tioga Pass. Allow about 90 minutes one-way without stops, or a full day with Olmsted Point, Tenaya Lake, and Tuolumne Meadows.

faq.q: How hard is the hike to the top of Half Dome?
faq.a: The full round trip is 14-16 miles with 4,800 feet of elevation gain from Happy Isles. Most hikers take 10-14 hours. The final 400 feet on the cables is a hands-on scramble on 45-degree granite. It ranks among the hardest day hikes in the national park system.

faq.q: Do I need a permit to hike Half Dome?
faq.a: Yes. A permit is required to hike past the base of the subdome to the summit. There are two lottery systems: a preseason lottery in March and a daily lottery during cables season. Without a permit, rangers at the subdome checkpoint will turn you back.

faq.q: What is Clouds Rest and is it a better hike than Half Dome?
faq.a: Clouds Rest is a 10-mile round trip from Tenaya Lake that gains about 1,750 feet to a summit at 9,926 feet, roughly 1,000 feet higher than Half Dome, with views of the entire park. No permit required. It is less crowded, costs nothing extra, and the view is broader.

faq.q: When are the cables up on Half Dome?
faq.a: Typically from the Friday before Memorial Day through the day after Columbus Day (the second Monday in October). The Park Service announces exact dates each year based on snow, weather, and crew availability.

faq.q: What should I bring to hike Half Dome?
faq.a: At least 3-4 liters of water, trail shoes with real traction (not sandals), sun protection, food for 12+ hours, a headlamp in case you run late, and gloves for the cables. Starting before sunrise is standard practice on this route.

faq.q: When does Glacier Point Road open in 2026?
faq.a: Glacier Point Road opened in early May 2026, ahead of the typical Memorial Day weekend opening. The road runs 16 miles from Highway 41 to the Glacier Point overlook at 7,214 feet.

faq.q: What is open at Glacier Point in early 2026?
faq.a: The overlook, restrooms, and trailheads for Sentinel Dome and Taft Point open with the road. The Glacier Point Snack Stand typically opens later in May or June. Bring all your food and water for early-season visits.

faq.q: What are the best hikes on Glacier Point Road?
faq.a: Sentinel Dome (2.2 miles round trip, 400 feet gain, 360-degree summit views), Taft Point (2.2 miles round trip, dramatic granite overhang above the Valley), and the start of the Panorama Trail toward Nevada Fall (8.5 miles one-way). All trailheads are along the road.

faq.q: How long is the drive on Glacier Point Road?
faq.a: About 16 miles one-way from the Highway 41 turnoff. Allow 30-40 minutes each way without stops. The road is narrow and winding with no passing lanes for most of its length.

faq.q: What is the elevation of Glacier Point?
faq.a: 7,214 feet. Half Dome's summit is at 8,839 feet. From the viewpoint, Half Dome appears roughly at eye level despite being about 1,600 feet higher, because the viewpoint itself sits on the valley rim.

faq.q: How hard is the Mist Trail?
faq.a: It depends on how far you go. The 1.6-mile round trip to the Vernal Fall footbridge is moderate. The 2.6-mile round trip to the top of Vernal Fall climbs 1,000 feet on wet granite stairs and is strenuous. The full 5.4-mile round trip to the top of Nevada Fall gains 2,000 feet and takes most people 4-6 hours.

faq.q: What shoes should I wear on the Mist Trail?
faq.a: Hiking boots or trail shoes with real tread. The granite staircase below Vernal Fall is wet for most of May and June, and slippery footwear is the cause of most Mist Trail injuries. Worn sneakers, flip-flops, and sandals are genuinely dangerous here.

faq.q: When is the Mist Trail wettest?
faq.a: Peak waterfall flow runs mid-April through late June, with the heaviest spray between the base and top of Vernal Fall in May. You'll get soaked, not sprinkled. By August the falls are reduced and the trail is mostly dry.

faq.q: Can kids hike the Mist Trail?
faq.a: Older, reasonably fit kids can do the 1.6-mile round trip to the Vernal Fall footbridge. Past the bridge, the staircase to the top of Vernal Fall is steep, wet, and exposed, not appropriate for young children. The full route to Nevada Fall is a serious workout.

faq.q: Can I die on the Mist Trail?
faq.a: People have. In 2025 roughly 30% of Yosemite's search-and-rescue operations originated on the Mist Trail corridor, and the park averages close to one fatality per month on this trail and the falls above it. Stay behind the railings and don't wade above either waterfall.

faq.q: Should I go up the Mist Trail and down the John Muir Trail?
faq.a: Yes if you're doing the full route to Nevada Fall. Up the Mist Trail for the waterfall experience, down the JMT for gentler grades that are easier on knees. Total loop is about 6.5 miles. Most experienced hikers do it this way.

faq.q: Who employs most of the workers in Yosemite?
faq.a: Not the National Park Service. Most jobs in the park, including lodging, food service, retail, shuttles, and front desk, are run by the authorized concessionaire, Yosemite Hospitality, a subsidiary of Aramark. NPS jobs are fewer and harder to land. Yosemite Conservancy hires a small team of seasonal naturalists, NatureBridge runs environmental education, and the Ansel Adams Gallery is tiny.

faq.q: What is employee housing in Yosemite like?
faq.a: Entry level is a 10-by-10 tent cabin at Curry Village shared with one to three roommates, with communal kitchens, bathrooms, and laundry, and a bear box on the porch. Rent is under twenty dollars a week, deducted from your paycheck. The housing ladder climbs to hard-walled cabins, dorm rooms, and eventually a solo room or studio, but the full climb takes years.

faq.q: Can you live in Yosemite without working there?
faq.a: No, with a few grandfathered exceptions. Living in the park requires working in the park, and working in the park does not always come with housing.

faq.q: Can Yosemite employees bring pets?
faq.a: Mostly no. Most park housing prohibits pets and most trails prohibit them too. Service animals are protected by law, and emotional support animals are allowed in housing but not at work or on the trails.

faq.q: How far is the nearest grocery store or hospital from Yosemite Valley?
faq.a: About an hour's drive. The closest grocery store with real selection is in Mariposa for most Valley residents, and the closest hospital, dentist, and eye doctor are all an hour or more away. A small clinic in the Valley handles routine care and stabilization.

faq.q: What is a water ouzel?
faq.a: The water ouzel, also called the American dipper (Cinclus mexicanus), is a dark, robin-sized songbird that walks underwater in cold, fast mountain streams and forages directly inside waterfalls. It is the most specialized stream bird in the Yosemite high country.

faq.q: How does a water ouzel survive inside a waterfall?
faq.a: It is built for it. Dense plumage waterproofed by an exceptionally effective oil gland, short powerful legs, sharp claws with specialized tendons that grip rock against the current, and eyes that focus underwater nearly as well as in air. It does not swim through the torrent; it walks the stream bottom.

faq.q: Where can I see a water ouzel in Yosemite?
faq.a: The bridge below Vernal Fall on the Mist Trail is one of the most reliable spots. The base of Yosemite Falls in early summer is another. Look for a compact, dark gray-brown bird moving in and out of fast water.

faq.q: What do water ouzels eat?
faq.a: Aquatic insects and their larvae, including mayfly, caddisfly, and stonefly larvae, plus small aquatic crustaceans. These insects live on the bottoms of cold, fast-moving, well-oxygenated streams, which is why the ouzel stays so close to cascades and falls.

faq.q: What does seeing a water ouzel tell you about a stream?
faq.a: That the stream is healthy. Ouzels require cold, fast-moving, well-oxygenated water with a rich population of specialized aquatic insects, so their presence confirms those conditions. Their absence from a stream where they were historically recorded signals that the water has become warmer, slower, or more degraded.

faq.q: When do black bears emerge from their dens in Yosemite?
faq.a: Bears begin emerging in April, after five to seven months in torpor. The trigger is not hunger but lengthening days and rising temperatures, which reset the bear's circadian rhythm and restart its metabolism. A bear that emerges in mid-April has spent the winter burning stored fat at roughly 25 percent of its normal metabolic rate.

faq.q: Why are Yosemite bears most dangerous in spring?
faq.a: Spring is when bears are most motivated, not most aggressive. A newly emerged bear has lost 20 to 40 percent of its body weight and faces acute caloric demand while only low-calorie spring vegetation is available. That metabolic urgency makes spring bears bolder: they hold their ground around humans, persist at food sources, and are more likely to attempt entry into cabins or food storage areas.

faq.q: What is torpor and how is it different from hibernation?
faq.a: Torpor is the near-hibernation state Yosemite bears enter in November or December. Heart rate drops from 70 to 100 beats per minute to 8 to 10, body temperature falls from about 38 degrees Celsius into the low 30s, the kidneys nearly shut down, and the bear neither eats, drinks, nor defecates. Unlike true hibernation, the bear can wake if disturbed.

faq.q: How should visitors behave around bears in spring?
faq.a: Spring requires the most rigorous food storage practices and bear-box discipline, since this is when bears most aggressively seek human food. Make noise on the trail to avoid surprise encounters, especially on lower Valley hikes like the Mist Trail where May and June foraging overlaps with peak hiking season.

faq.q: Does Yosemite still have glaciers?
faq.a: Yes. Four glaciers remain: Mount Lyell (the largest and lowest descending), Mount Dana, Mount Maclure, and a handful of smaller cirque accumulations on the Cathedral Range. Most sit above 10,000 feet, and all are reached from Tioga Road, so visits are seasonal, roughly late June through October.

faq.q: How much have Yosemite's glaciers retreated?
faq.a: All four have retreated significantly since a 1933 survey, most by more than half their length. Mount Lyell's terminus has moved from about 9,500 feet of elevation in 1933 to near 9,900 feet today, meaning the glacier has thinned as well as shortened. A cairn a ranger built at the 1933 terminus now sits roughly 400 feet downslope from the ice.

faq.q: Why are the glaciers shrinking?
faq.a: The High Sierra has warmed by roughly 1.5 degrees Celsius since 1900, with most of that concentrated in recent decades and summer temperatures warming more than winter. An upslope retreat of a glacier's terminus signals either less snow accumulation or more summer melt; either way it points to a warmed climate, consistent with what climate models project.

faq.q: Why do the glaciers matter for California's water?
faq.a: About half of California's fresh water comes from the Sierra Nevada, much of it from snowmelt and glacier melt. Glaciers act as high-elevation reservoirs, storing winter snow as ice and releasing it gradually through summer melt to sustain streams like the Tenaya, Merced, and Tuolumne. As glaciers shrink, July and August streamflow will gradually decline and cold-water aquatic ecosystems will be stressed.

faq.q: Why do giant sequoias need fire?
faq.a: Fire clears competing vegetation and exposes the bare mineral soil that tiny sequoia seeds need to establish, and it opens the canopy to give seedlings light. In a fire-suppressed forest, shade-tolerant species like white fir colonize the understory, the canopy closes, and sequoia seedlings are starved of light. A sequoia grove without fire is a grove in slow decline.

faq.q: How do giant sequoias survive fires that kill other trees?
faq.a: Mature sequoia bark can be two feet thick, loose and fibrous so it barely conducts heat, and rich in tannin that resists flame. When fire passes, the outer bark chars and that charring insulates the living wood beneath. Thinner-barked trees like white fir and sugar pine can be killed by ten or twenty minutes of sustained ground-fire heat, while the sequoia survives with only a scar.

faq.q: How often did fire burn in the Mariposa Grove?
faq.a: A 1929 fire-scar survey documented in Nature Notes counted at least two major burns per century over the past two thousand years. Trees that germinated in the 1600s grew in a forest that burned roughly every ten to thirty years; a single two-thousand-year-old sequoia may carry eight or ten distinct fire scars.

faq.q: Why did Yosemite change its fire policy?
faq.a: For about 150 years the park tried to prevent all fire, which let fuel accumulate and shade-tolerant species crowd the understory, leaving groves unable to regenerate and primed for hotter, more destructive fires. Land managers now treat fire as a necessity and run carefully timed, low-intensity restoration burns in groves like Mariposa, Tuolumne, and Merced to mimic the natural fire regime.

faq.q: How do I get to Hetch Hetchy in Yosemite?
faq.a: Take Highway 120 west to Evergreen Road (about 1 mile past the Big Oak Flat entrance station), then Hetch Hetchy Road 16 miles to O'Shaughnessy Dam. The road has a gate with set hours, so check nps.gov/yose before driving out. The round trip from Yosemite Valley is about 3-4 hours including driving.

faq.q: Can you hike to Wapama Falls at Hetch Hetchy?
faq.a: Yes. The Wapama Falls trail is 4.8 miles round trip from the dam, gaining about 500 feet. In peak snowmelt (April-May) the crossing at the falls can be knee-deep and is sometimes closed. In summer it's a dry footbridge crossing. The falls are dramatically higher in May than in August.

faq.q: Is Hetch Hetchy crowded?
faq.a: Far less than Yosemite Valley. On a busy weekend, Hetch Hetchy sees a fraction of Valley traffic. The gated road hours limit early-morning surge further. If the Valley is slammed, Hetch Hetchy offers a wild Yosemite experience with essentially no wait.

faq.q: Why was Hetch Hetchy Valley flooded?
faq.a: In 1913 Congress passed the Raker Act authorizing O'Shaughnessy Dam, despite John Muir's national campaign to protect the valley. San Francisco needed a reliable water supply, and the valley's remote location inside federal land made it the proposed reservoir site. Muir called it a desecration equal to flooding the Sistine Chapel.

faq.q: Can Hetch Hetchy be restored?
faq.a: Engineering studies show the valley could be drained and would recover ecologically within decades. The political challenge is substantial: San Francisco still draws water and hydroelectric power from the reservoir. Replacement infrastructure would take years and billions of dollars. Restoration legislation is periodically introduced in Sacramento.

faq.q: Where is the best stargazing in Yosemite?
faq.a: Olmsted Point and Glacier Point are the most accessible high-altitude sites, both above 7,000 feet, away from Valley light, with wide sky exposure. Tuolumne Meadows has longer horizon lines. Sentinel Dome is excellent for Milky Way photography. The Valley floor has noticeably more light pollution than any of these.

faq.q: When is the best time to stargaze in Yosemite?
faq.a: New moon weekends from late July through September. The Milky Way core is highest in August, which is also the driest, warmest month for high-country nights. Use a moon phase calendar and timeanddate.com moonrise tables to find nights when the moon sets before midnight.

faq.q: Is there a Yosemite Star Party?
faq.a: Yes. The Yosemite Conservancy organizes annual stargazing programs at Glacier Point, typically in late summer, with telescopes and astronomy interpreters. Tickets are limited and sell out early, so check yosemite.org for dates and registration.

faq.q: Can you see the Milky Way from Yosemite Valley?
faq.a: On a moonless night, yes, but the Valley's lodging and village lighting reduce contrast. The high-country sites, Olmsted Point, Glacier Point, and Sentinel Dome, offer dramatically better views with comparable drive time from most gateway towns.

faq.q: What should I bring for stargazing in Yosemite?
faq.a: Warm layers (high-country nights drop to 40F even in August), a red-light flashlight to preserve night vision, a blanket or camp chair for lying back, and binoculars, which reveal far more than the naked eye without telescope setup. A free app like Stellarium helps identify constellations and planets.

faq.q: Is Yosemite worth visiting if you don't hike?
faq.a: Absolutely. The most dramatic viewpoints, Tunnel View, El Capitan Meadow, Valley View, Glacier Point, and Olmsted Point, are all drive-up or involve short paved walks under half a mile. The Valley tram tour, Mariposa Grove tram, and in-park shuttle require no hiking.

faq.q: What can you see in Yosemite without hiking?
faq.a: Tunnel View (drive-up), El Capitan and Yosemite Falls from roadside meadows, Bridalveil Fall (0.5-mile paved path), Lower Yosemite Fall loop (1-mile paved loop), Valley View (pull-out), Glacier Point overlook (drive-up), Olmsted Point (Tioga Road pull-out), and Mariposa Grove (tram tour available).

faq.q: Are there guided tours in Yosemite for non-hikers?
faq.a: Yes. The Yosemite Valley Floor Tour is a 2-hour open-air tram covering the main Valley viewpoints. Glacier Point bus tours run daily in summer. The Mariposa Grove tram offers a narrated circuit through the sequoia grove. All are operated by the park concessionaire, bookable at yosemite.com.

faq.q: Is Glacier Point accessible without hiking?
faq.a: Yes. Glacier Point is a drive-up viewpoint with a paved overlook and restrooms. No hiking is required to reach the main viewpoint. In summer, a bus tour from the Valley also serves it for those who do not want to drive the narrow 16-mile road.

faq.q: Can you visit Yosemite by bus or train?
faq.a: Yes. Amtrak's San Joaquin line runs to Merced, where YARTS buses make the 2-hour trip to Yosemite Valley. YARTS runs year-round on the Highway 140/Merced route. In summer, YARTS also connects Lee Vining and Mammoth Lakes to the Valley via Tioga Road.

faq.q: What should I pack in my car for a Yosemite trip?
faq.a: A well-packed cooler, a rigid water jug of four to seven gallons, layers (fleece, rain jacket, warm hat) for every person, a paper park map and offline maps, and a roadside kit with a portable jump starter, spare tire, and flashlight. Binoculars, a windshield sunshade, and camp chairs earn their space too.

faq.q: Do I need to store food in my car in Yosemite because of bears?
faq.a: Yes. Any food or scented item, including sealed coolers, granola bars, gum, sunscreen, and chapstick, must be stored properly. In campgrounds it goes in the bear box. At trailheads keep it in the trunk, out of sight, with windows closed. Bears recognize coolers through windows and peel doors open.

faq.q: How long will a cooler stay cold in Yosemite?
faq.a: Three to four days if it stays shut and in the shade in the trunk. A cooler that is opened every thirty minutes and sits in the back seat in July lasts about eight hours. Pack in layers and freeze water bottles to use as ice blocks and cold drinking water.

faq.q: Is there cell service in Yosemite for navigation?
faq.a: Not reliably outside the Valley. Carry the free paper park map and download offline maps over wifi before you enter. There is no gas between Lee Vining and Crane Flat, about 60 miles, so fill up before entering from any direction.

faq.q: What roadside gear should I bring to Yosemite?
faq.a: A portable jump starter (dead batteries are common at elevation), a spare tire with the tools and the know-how to change it, a basic tool kit with duct tape and zip ties, and a real flashlight that works when your phone is dead. Tows can be hours away.

faq.q: Which Yosemite gateway town is closest to the Valley?
faq.a: El Portal, about 14 miles and 25-30 minutes from Yosemite Valley via Highway 140. Mariposa is next at 45 miles and 45-60 minutes. Lee Vining is closest to Tuolumne Meadows (about 30 minutes) but 90+ minutes from the Valley.

faq.q: Which Yosemite gateway town is best for first-time visitors?
faq.a: Mariposa, for most first-timers. It pairs a real town (groceries, dinner, lodging at several price points) with the reliable, year-round Highway 140 approach. El Portal is closer if you can get a room, but Mariposa is the better all-round balance of cost and convenience.

faq.q: Which Yosemite gateway town is cheapest?
faq.a: Groveland and Mariposa typically have the widest price range and the most budget options. El Portal lodging is priced like in-park lodging because of the location. Oakhurst has predictable chain prices. Lee Vining has limited inventory and is priced accordingly.

faq.q: Which Yosemite gateway town is best for families?
faq.a: Mariposa, by a wide margin. It has full-service grocery stores, multiple restaurants, a wide range of lodging from budget motels to inns, and a real downtown to spend an evening in. The 45-minute drive to the Valley is a fair trade for the amenities.

faq.q: Which Yosemite gateway towns have full grocery stores?
faq.a: Mariposa and Oakhurst have full grocery stores. Groveland has a smaller one. El Portal has a market, not a real grocery. Lee Vining has limited groceries. Stock up at the larger town before you head in.

faq.q: Do Yosemite gateway towns have reliable cell service?
faq.a: Patchy in all five gateways and essentially nonexistent inside the park past Crane Flat. Don't rely on real-time Google Maps once you're past the entrance station. Download offline maps before you leave the gateway.

faq.q: When is smoke season at Yosemite?
faq.a: Smoke season in California overlaps fire season: July through October. August and September are the most affected months on average, though clear stretches happen throughout and forecasts are unreliable beyond 48-72 hours.

faq.q: How do I check air quality before visiting Yosemite?
faq.a: AirNow.gov (EPA) is the standard source. The Yosemite NPS website posts air quality advisories. Check the AQI for the Yosemite Valley area 48-72 hours before departure and again the morning you travel, since conditions change fast during fire season.

faq.q: Should I wear a mask in Yosemite smoke?
faq.a: If AQI is above 100, an N95 or KN95 mask provides meaningful protection, especially for children, the elderly, and anyone with respiratory conditions. Surgical masks and cloth masks do not filter fine smoke particles effectively.

faq.q: What is a good alternative if Yosemite is too smoky?
faq.a: The eastern Sierra often has better air when prevailing winds carry smoke away from the park. Mono Lake, Mammoth Lakes, and the June Lake Loop are worth checking. Smoke also typically clears after cold fronts, so monitoring the forecast 48-72 hours out gives you a real window to reschedule.

faq.q: Does wildfire smoke ruin a Yosemite trip?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Haze produces warm, diffused light that photographers actively seek. On moderate-smoke days (AQI 50-100) most outdoor activities are fine for healthy adults. On heavy-smoke days (AQI 150+) strenuous outdoor exercise is not recommended, so use the time for indoor sites, driving routes, or the Ahwahnee.

faq.q: Do you need a permit to propose in Yosemite?
faq.a: No. The park draws a clear line between proposals and weddings: a proposal is a personal moment between two people, with no permit, fee, or paperwork required. Weddings are different and require a Special Use Permit from the NPS.

faq.q: Do you need a photography permit for a Yosemite proposal?
faq.a: No, in most cases. The EXPLORE Act of 2025 eliminated the photography permit requirement for groups of eight or fewer on public lands, so a couple plus a hired photographer is covered, as long as the total group stays at eight or under and you are not using props, sets, or models.

faq.q: What is the best place to propose in Yosemite?
faq.a: The naturalist's own pick is North Dome, which looks straight across at Half Dome from eye level and is often empty on a weekday. For privacy in the Valley, Cathedral Beach on the Merced River is the most recommended spot. Glacier Point has the most famous view but is best at sunrise to avoid the crowds.

faq.q: Are decorations or drones allowed for a Yosemite proposal?
faq.a: No. The National Park Service prohibits decorations, rose petals, candles, balloon arches, confetti, streamers, and signs staked into meadows. Drones are also banned and carry a fine of up to $5,000.

faq.q: When is the best time to propose in Yosemite?
faq.a: Early morning and late afternoon beat midday at every popular viewpoint for light and crowds. Spring (late April through early June) brings peak waterfalls, October offers golden oaks and thin crowds, and mid-to-late February can deliver the Horsetail Fall Firefall near Valentine's Day. For night proposals, aim for a new moon in the high country from late May through September.
